prose_edits.before: Replacing a dense projection with two smaller matrices offers a direct way to reduce stored weights. The difficult question is whether those replacements preserve the behavior of the complete model. A projection can reconstruct its teacher outputs on calibration inputs yet encounter different activations after earlier projections have also been replaced. Conversely, an altered model can improve held-out next-token likelihood while moving farther from the teacher's internal representations. These outcomes test different properties and should not be summarized by a single compression score.
prose_edits.after: Language models use weight matrices to transform text into predictions. Low-rank compression replaces a large matrix with two smaller factors. The replacement saves weights, but its effect depends on the rest of the model. A factorized layer may closely match the original on calibration inputs and still receive different inputs after earlier layers have been compressed. A compressed model may also predict text more accurately while its internal representations move farther from those of the original model, which we call the teacher. We measure these outcomes separately.

prose_edits.before: We ask: **at a fixed factor budget, does adding a weight-space anchor to activation-weighted low-rank fitting consistently improve both held-out likelihood and residual-state fidelity, and what storage and execution benefit remains?** The anchor changes the fitting objective without adding an inference branch. This makes it a controlled comparison against unanchored covariance weighting, rather than a comparison between differently sized representations.
prose_edits.after: We test whether a weight-space anchor improves prediction quality and internal similarity when the number of stored factor weights is fixed. Activation weighting gives more importance to input directions observed during calibration. The anchor adds a penalty for changing the original weights. It changes how the factors are fitted but adds no branch at inference. We compare it with covariance weighting without the anchor, using the same factor budget, and measure storage and execution cost.

prose_edits.before: Our contribution is a bounded empirical analysis with three parts. First, we distinguish activation weighting, anchoring and extra ridge shrinkage mathematically and compare their recorded controls. Second, we examine complete attention-output stacks and consecutive groups, keeping likelihood and propagated residual drift separate. Third, we distinguish targeted parameter savings from serialized whole-model size and measured runtime. The results expose useful failures: average improvements need not reproduce across seeds or groups, and better likelihood can accompany substantially greater drift.
prose_edits.after: The study separates the effects of activation weighting, anchoring and extra ridge shrinkage. We test attention-output replacements across the full stack and in consecutive groups, measuring prediction quality alongside the changes that propagate through the residual stream. We also measure complete checkpoint size and runtime. The results show where an average joint improvement fails to hold across calibration seeds or layer groups, and where better prediction quality accompanies greater internal drift.

prose_edits.before: This is an exploratory study, rather than a claim of a new whitening algorithm or a solved global-preservation problem. The strict numerical-readiness checks were not uniformly satisfied. The Qwen primary comparison is available, but its validation frontier is incomplete. The later BF16 practical cohort has only two calibration seeds and adds no BF16 drift measurement. We retain those boundaries throughout the analysis.
prose_edits.after: The results remain exploratory. Some strict numerical accuracy checks failed, and Qwen's primary comparison is available without a complete validation rank frontier. The later practical cohort uses bfloat16 (BF16), has only two calibration seeds, and adds no BF16 drift measurements. We do not claim a new whitening algorithm or reliable preservation of the complete model's computation.

prose_edits.before: The results distinguish three questions. A representation can be smaller than its dense source, fit a data distribution better than a comparator, and still diverge from the teacher internally. None of these outcomes logically supplies the others. In particular, the LFM observation is evidence against using likelihood improvement alone as a preservation certificate. It is not evidence that residual similarity is always the correct optimization target: $D$ measures similarity in fixed coordinates, while different internal states can implement similar functions. A future claim about global preservation needs converging evidence from final logits, tasks, drift and generation rather than privileging one proxy.
prose_edits.after: LFM predicts text better under the anchored fit while its residual representations differ more from the teacher's. This result limits what likelihood alone can tell us about preservation. Residual similarity also has limits: $D$ compares states in fixed coordinates, and different states can implement similar functions. A stronger preservation claim needs agreement across final logits, task performance, drift measurements and generation tests. Smaller storage or a better score on one measure does not supply that evidence.

prose_edits.before: The strongest comparison for anchoring is matched covariance weighting. Large gains over plain SVD primarily establish the importance of data-aware fitting within this implementation; they do not establish the incremental value or novelty of the anchor. Gemma's small average advantage, Qwen's joint worsening and LFM's tradeoff do not support a model-independent recommendation to add the same anchor. Because model weights, tokenizers, mixer structures and historical inference precision differ, this study cannot attribute the different outcomes solely to architecture.
prose_edits.after: Matched covariance weighting is the relevant baseline for the anchor. Gains over plain SVD show the value of data-aware fitting in this implementation, but cannot establish what the anchor adds or whether it is novel. Gemma's small average advantage, Qwen's joint worsening and LFM's tradeoff provide no consistent basis for adding the same anchor across models. The models also differ in pretrained weights, tokenizers, mixers and historical inference precision, so we cannot attribute those outcomes solely to architecture.

prose_edits.before: At the measured attention-output budgets, activation-aware low-rank fitting improves on plain SVD, but anchoring does not consistently improve both likelihood and propagated residual fidelity over matched whitening. Gemma's small full-stack average change does not transfer uniformly to layer groups; Qwen worsens on both metrics; LFM improves likelihood while increasing drift. The separate BF16 practical cohort achieves a measured 0.894% whole-checkpoint saving with mixed timing. These findings support reporting likelihood, teacher-state fidelity and practical cost as distinct outcomes. Reliable preservation of global computation remains unresolved.
prose_edits.after: Activation-aware low-rank fitting improves on plain SVD at the tested attention-output budgets. Adding the anchor provides no consistent joint improvement in likelihood and residual fidelity over matched whitening. Gemma's small average gain does not hold across all layer groups. Qwen worsens on both metrics, while LFM improves likelihood and increases drift. The separate BF16 practical cohort saves 0.894% of the complete checkpoint size and has mixed timing results. Compression remains unproven as a way to preserve the original computation across the tested models.
